sentences.text: The CMS AI and Copyright Case Tracker is a database compiled by the law firm CMS that summarizes 23 court cases on AI and copyright from 10 jurisdictions, led by Germany (MMRS record); its makers call it "a copyright + AI case tracker providing accessible, easily digestible case summaries, updated regularly, covering the most topical case law in the area of AI and copyright", built "with our CMS colleagues across UK, Europe and beyond" (cms.law, the tracker's page), a publication dated 31 Oct 2025 in the site's International edition.

Its unit is the case, the "court case on AI and copyright" (MMRS record), each with a summary page that "provides details of the relevant litigation, including summaries of each party’s arguments and the final judgment" (cms.law), its fields in the MMRS record case name, jurisdiction, date, the litigation, each party's arguments and the judgment; the two case pages on the rail carry court, country, parties, the date the claim was issued and the type of claim (the India and UK pages).

It is "compiled by the firm's lawyers across jurisdictions", with CMS (law firm) its operator (MMRS record): the index page names Sarah Wright, Partner and Co-Head of Intellectual Property, and Ben Hitchens, Partner, in London as its contacts, and the India page Bharadwaj Jaishankar, Partner, CMS Induslaw, in Bengaluru.

Wikipedia has no article for it ("Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name.", and a search for 'Copyright Case Tracker' finds "no results"); its article on the operator describes CMS as "an international law firm that offers legal and tax advisory services", consisting "of 18 independent law firms, with about 80 offices worldwide", formed in 1999 by six European firms under a brand joining Cameron McKenna (UK) and Hasche Sigle (Germany).

The index lists "23 Pages", newest first, each entry headed by its jurisdiction, from "1. Germany - GEMA v. Suno, 31 July 2026" to "23. Czech Republic - S. Š. v TAUBEL LEGAL, advokátní kancelář s.r.o. , 11 October 2023" (cms.law); read whole, its entries come from ten jurisdictions, Germany with eight, and none is a US case, which the MMRS record counts as "23 cases in 10 jurisdictions (no US cases listed)", the jurisdictions Germany, the UK, the Netherlands, Hungary, China, France, Italy, India, Austria and the Czech Republic, the newest entry dated 31 July 2026.

The page says its summaries are "updated regularly", and the MMRS record gives the cadence by that phrase and the newest entry's date; the pages carry their own dates beside their status dates: the index 31 Oct 2025, the India page 25 Jun 2025 with its status as on 24 July 2026, the UK page 27 Sep 2024 with its status as at 5 January 2026.

The executive summary frames the field: generative AI has "brought to fore many new legal issues relating to ownership, subsistence and infringement of copyright law", and, it says, "At the heart of the discourse is the reinterpretation of copyright principles in the age of AI-generated content" (cms.law).

It names three questions UK and European courts are grappling with, each tied to a tracked case: an infringement claim where a whole work is copied "for the purpose of training a large language model" but outputs contain only "“infinitesimally small” reproductions" (Getty Images v Stability AI), a training dataset "using only transient copies of the original work" (Robert Kneschke v LAION), and authorship where the law may define the author as a "“natural person”" (S. Š. v TAUBEL LEGAL); and it expects the area to be "increasingly complicated by newer and more advanced technologies, and the implementation of the EU AI Act" (cms.law).

On the United States the page speaks of the field, and its list holds no US entry: US courts "have led the way in AI & copyright litigation to date", with similar claims beginning before UK and European courts; "There are now over 40 copyright claims being litigated in the US", among them Disney and NBC Universal against Midjourney and the pending New York Times v OpenAI, Dow Jones v Perplexity and Getty v Stability AI; and in June 2025 a Californian court ruled that training Claude on books did not infringe, while Anthropic must face trial over pirated materials (cms.law).

The MMRS record keeps that sentence apart from the list: "the page's summary states that 'there are now over 40 copyright claims being litigated in the US'; none is in the tracked list"; and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) finds that the record's count "stands, and now quotes the sentence".

The page's region selector, "Select your region" with International, Europe, Africa, Asia-Pacific, The Americas and Middle East, is the site's navigation, its lists opening onto the countries of the firm's sites and offices, the Americas list ending with the United States of America, whose link leads to the firm's Silicon Valley office page (cms.law); the MMRS record notes that the menu "leads to the firm's offices".

Cases not yet summarised may be sent to the firm by email (cms.law), "uncovered cases" to "a submission address" in the MMRS record; and the page sets beside the tracker a sibling tool for "digital regulations in the EU and in the world", the firm's "digital regulation hub and brand new digital Regulation Tracker tool" (cms.law).

Of the tracked cases, ANI Media Pvt Ltd v OpenAI OPCO LLC (Delhi High Court, claim issued 19 November 2024) reached an interim order on 24 July 2026 refusing ANI's injunction and "holding that at the prima facie stage, OpenAI’s use of ANI’s content to train ChatGPT models falls under the ‘fair dealing’ exception"; "the main suit continues to be heard on merits" (the India page).

The court's fair dealing test had three factors, whether use was "limited to LLM training", market competition or prejudice, and "a broader public interest"; it held, prima facie, that the responses complained of came not from memorisation but from "the RAG technique, through which LLMs retrieve relevant information from external sources"; and ANI's claim was that ChatGPT "gives false information as output and cites the ANI’s news agency as its source" (the India page).

In Getty Images v Stability AI (High Court of England & Wales, claim issued 15 January 2023) the judgment of 4 November 2025 "rejected Getty’s secondary copyright claim in full", finding that an AI model may in principle be an "“article”" under s.22 CDPA 1988 but that "Stable Diffusion did not embody any infringing copies of Getty works", its weights operating "at a high level of mathematical abstraction that does not encode, contain, or allow extraction of any specific image"; Getty had dropped its primary copyright and database right claims late in the trial and won only "a narrow set of trade mark issues", and the page says Stability "was granted leave to appeal the secondary infringement claim on 17 December 2025" (the UK page).

The firm reads the judgment as "the first detailed judicial assessment in the UK of secondary copyright infringement in the context of AI model weights" that "significantly limits the circumstances in which AI developers may incur liability" (the UK page); the same page calls Stable Diffusion "a deep-learning, text-to-image (and now image-to-image) AI model", where the index's question set the case under "training a large language model" (cms.law).

In the MMRS record the tracker "records the legal reception of the provenance question: what courts decide about training on, and outputting, protected work", its role provenance by the record's reading; "With no US cases listed, it sits beside the US litigation trackers, which were not read for this census" (MMRS record).

The question stands in the cases as the field gives them: ANI's complaint that a model cites the agency as the source of false information, and the Delhi court's prima facie finding that the responses came by retrieval from external sources (the India page), beside the record's reading of the tracker as the legal reception of provenance (MMRS record).

A second tracker of the same name stands on the same rail and is a distinct entity: Taylor Wessing's "AI & Copyright Case Tracker", whose card lists "Carlsen v. OpenAI, Penguin v. OpenAI, GEMA v. OpenAI, GEMA v. Suno, Koda v. Suno AI, SNE v. Meta", its page refused (403) and unread, two of its cases, GEMA v. Suno and GEMA v OpenAI, also in CMS's list (cms.law); the MMRS record carries it as a neighbour and census candidate, listed "for reading", which enters the census "once it has been read at its own pages", and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) as "another aggregator; added as a candidate".

The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity: "each page has two nodes, the MMRS record and the entity it describes", each assertion with a source and a basis, the lifecycle kept apart from the observation that saw it; the tracker's state is active, observed on 2026-10-28 by reading, with the index page the one source for all fields (MMRS record).

The composition layer's account at the tracker's name, of 2026-10-29, is seated in the Capture Registry and held by the MMRS record as a relation of the entity (MMRS record); the Registry finds the Overview's five regions to be "the page's region selector, which leads to CMS's offices", and that "The tracked cases are European, with China and India" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the selector is the menu the page heads "Select your region" (cms.law).

It finds that "'Over 40 U.S. claims' is the page's summary sentence" and that "no US case is in the tracker's list", and reads the composition as one that "reads a law firm's page whole, navigation and summary with the list, and composes the tracker's reach from the firm's office menu and the US count from a sentence about the field" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), the page's sentence being "There are now over 40 copyright claims being litigated in the US" (cms.law).

"The cases it names are right": Getty v. Stability AI, Kneschke v. LAION and ANI v. OpenAI are in CMS's pages, the last "with its interim order of 24 July 2026" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), as the list's entries and the India page give them (cms.law; the India page).

translation.lineage: case: ANI Media v OpenAI (Delhi High Court)
translation.received: F20 (B2, publication header): "Publication India - ANI Media Pvt Ltd V. OpenAI OPCO LLC, 24 July 2026 25 Jun 2025 International"; F21 (B2, case fields): "Court Delhi High Court Country India Parties Claimant: ANI Media Pvt Ltd Defendant: OpenAI OPCO LLC Date Claim Issued 19 November 2024 Type of Claim Copyright infringement claim"; F22 (B2, Status as on 24 July 2026 ¶4): "On 24 July 2026, the DHC passed an interim order refusing ANI’s request for an interim injunction, holding that at the prima facie stage, OpenAI’s use of ANI’s content to train ChatGPT models falls under the ‘fair dealing’ exception under Section 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act."; F23 (B2, Summary of Key Background Facts, last ¶): "the DHC delivered its first substantive ruling in the matter, declining to grant ANI interim relief and holding that OpenAI’s training-related use of ANI’s content is, at the prima facie stage, protected by the fair dealing exception; the main suit continues to be heard on merits."; F24 (B2, The Court's Findings, fair dealing ¶2): "formulated a three-factor assessment for the present case: (i) whether the use of ANI’s works was limited to LLM training; (ii) whether such use resulted in market competition or prejudice to ANI’s legitimate commercial interests; and (iii) whether ChatGPT’s functions served a broader public interest."; F25 (B2, The Court's Findings, infringement ¶2): "held, prima facie, that the responses in question could not have resulted from memorisation of ANI’s works during training but rather using the RAG technique, through which LLMs retrieve relevant information from external sources."; F26 (B2, Summary of key legal arguments, ANI's Claims ¶2): "ANI claim that ChatGPT gives false information as output and cites the ANI’s news agency as its source, thereby posing a threat to its reputation and leading to the spread of misinformation in the digital sphere."
